sections.title: Joining a leisure centre
sections.context: You will hear a woman talking to a receptionist at a leisure centre in Manchester about joining.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Good morning, Wythenshawe Leisure Centre. This is Daniel. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Hello. I'd like to join the gym, please. I've just started a new job nearby, and I want to get fit.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Great. I can help you with that. Let me open the membership form. Could I have your name, please?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Yes. Priya Kowalczyk.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Sorry, how do you spell your surname?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: It's a little unusual. K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K. My husband is Polish.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K. Thank you, Mrs Kowalczyk. Now, there are several types of membership. Would you like full membership? That gives you the gym, the pool and all the classes, at any time.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Actually, wait. I'll probably only be able to come in the daytime, because I work evenings on three days a week. Do you have something cheaper for that?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: We do. It's called off-peak membership. You can use everything between nine in the morning and four in the afternoon, and after eight at night. It's a good choice if your hours are flexible.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: That sounds better. I'll take the off-peak one.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Lovely. The full price for that is £35 a month. But are you a student, or over sixty?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I'm actually doing a part-time degree, so I have a student card.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Then you get a discount. With a student card, it's £28 a month.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: That's good. Is there a joining fee?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Normally there is. It's £25. But we have an offer this month, so you pay only £15. I'd join now if I were you.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Then I'll join today, in that case. What happens next?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Every new member has a free induction. A member of staff will show you the equipment and write a personal programme for you. It takes about forty minutes. Do you want to book that now?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Yes, please. Could I come on Monday?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Hmm, Mondays are fully booked, I'm afraid, because it's the busiest day. We have places on Tuesday, though.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Tuesday is fine, actually. Even better, because I finish early that day.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: And what time would suit you?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Any time after about six, I think.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: I have a gap at 6:45. Would that work?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: That's perfect.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Brilliant. I'll put you down for 6:45 on Tuesday. Now, are there any classes you're interested in? We have spinning, aerobics, boxing and yoga.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I'd love to try yoga. I've done a little at home, but I'd like a proper teacher.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: The evening yoga class is very popular, so book early. But you can take it with your off-peak card, as it starts at 8:15.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Wonderful. And what about the pool? I'd like to swim in the mornings.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Lane swimming starts at 6:30 in the morning, but your membership only covers the pool after nine. If you'd like early swimming, you would have to upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: No, that's fine. I'll swim later in the day. Is there somewhere to leave my things while I'm training?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Yes, there are lockers in the changing rooms. You need a pound coin, which you get back when you open the locker. We also have a café on the first floor, and the hot showers are free.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Lovely. And do you have parking?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: There's a large car park at the front. The first two hours are free for members, but you must enter your registration at the desk.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Good. Now, I need your address for the membership card.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: It's 12 Ashby Road, Manchester.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Could you spell Ashby?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: A-S-H-B-Y.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Thank you. And the postcode?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: M14 6TQ. That's M, then 1-4, and then 6-T-Q.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: M14 6TQ. Got it. We also need an emergency contact, in case you have an accident.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I'll put my brother. His name is Marek, that's M-A-R-E-K.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Marek. And his phone number?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: I'll have to look for it. I don't remember it. Can I give it to you on Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Of course. Just bring it with you, together with your student card. Oh, and a pair of clean trainers. We ask everyone to use different shoes in the gym than they wear in the street.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Right. I'll remember that.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Thank you very much for calling, Mrs Kowalczyk. We'll see you on Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Thank you, Daniel. Goodbye.

sections.title: A new cycle path in Cambridge
sections.context: You will hear a council officer talking to residents about a new cycle path along the river in Cambridge.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name is Hugh Marlowe, and I'm the transport officer at the county council. Tonight I'd like to explain our plans for the Riverside Greenway, a new cycle path along the River Cam. I'll talk for about fifteen minutes, and then I'll be happy to answer your questions.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Let me start with the timetable. The plan was to open the path at the end of March, and you may have seen that date in the local newspaper. Unfortunately, the heavy rain this winter flooded the site, and the building work has been delayed by several weeks. We're now aiming to open the whole path in June. That's a firm date, and we have the contractors' agreement.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: The path will be nine kilometres long, from the railway station in the south to the village of Waterbeach in the north. Some people have asked why it isn't longer. We did consider extending it to eleven kilometres, but that would have meant crossing private land, and negotiations with the owners would have taken years. Nine kilometres is a good start, and we hope we can add more later.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: As for the cost, the total is about four million pounds. The largest part, around sixty per cent, comes from a government grant for sustainable transport. The council contributes about a third, and the rest has been donated by local businesses, including the college and the science park. I'd like to thank all of them for their support.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Let me now describe the route, starting at the station. As you leave the station, you'll find covered cycle parking for four hundred bikes. At the moment, as many of you know, the racks are always full, and bikes are left leaning against the railings. The new shelter will solve that problem. It also has cameras, so your bicycle will be safe.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: From there the path runs north, along the old railway line, until it reaches the river at the Mill Bridge. This is the most expensive part of the project. The old bridge is too narrow and in poor condition, so we are replacing it with a new wide bridge with two lanes, one in each direction. It will be built of steel and wood, and local designers have been involved.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Past the bridge, the path crosses Riverside Meadow. This is a beautiful area, and the wildlife groups were worried about the effect of the path. We listened to their concerns, and as a result we've made a small pond beside the track. It will attract frogs, dragonflies and water birds, and we'll put up information boards for walkers and families.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Some residents asked for a separate lane for walkers, but there isn't room on the Meadow. The existing footpath stays where it is, and the cycle path runs beside it, and the two are divided by a low hedge. We also thought about putting benches along the route, but we have decided to wait and see where people actually stop. We can add them later.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Next comes Orchard Lane. This is a quiet road, but it's dark in the evening, because the trees are tall and there are no street lights. The council is installing new lights along the full length of the lane. They are low energy, and they will only turn on when someone is nearby. So the lane will be safe in winter, without disturbing the neighbours with a bright glare all night.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: The last part of the path leads into the market area. This is where cyclists and pedestrians will mix, so we have introduced a few rules. When you reach the market, please get off your bike and walk. It is only a couple of hundred metres. A small bell is welcome, but it's not enough on its own. At the entrance to the market we'll install a repair stand with a pump and basic tools, which anyone can use free of charge.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Now, a word about how you can have your say. We held a public meeting last week, and about one hundred and fifty people attended. But we know not everyone can come in the evening, so we've also set up an online survey, which will stay open until the thirtieth of this month. The address is on the leaflets by the door. Please fill it in, because the results will help us decide on the details, such as where to put the signs.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: Finally, safety. The advisory speed on the path will be ten miles an hour. This is not a race track, and it's meant for families as well as commuters. We'll review the arrangements after the first year, and we'll make changes if there are problems.

transcript.speaker: Hugh
transcript.text: I know many of you have questions, and I'm sure some of you are worried about noise and traffic during the construction. I'll cover those in a moment. First, does anybody have a question about the route itself?

sections.title: Preparing a presentation on a Victorian novel
sections.context: You will hear two literature students discussing a presentation on a nineteenth century novel with their tutor.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Come in, Zainab. Hello, Tom. Sit down. You wanted to talk about your presentation on Great Expectations. Let's hear what you have so far.

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: Thank you, Dr Brennan. We chose the novel because it's the one we both enjoyed most on the course. I'd read it as a teenager, and I wanted to see whether I'd understand it differently now.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: For me it was partly the film. I saw a film version first, and it made me curious about the original.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Many students come to Dickens that way. Be careful, though, with the film. Some details are quite different from the book, and the examiners notice that.

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: That's what I said to Tom. I think we should refer only to the text.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: I agree. I was thinking of showing a short clip, but I think it would take too much time.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Good. And which edition are you using?

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: The one from the course reading list.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Quote page numbers from that same edition, so that nobody gets confused. You have twenty minutes, including questions. What are you going to focus on?

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: We discussed several themes. At first we thought of guilt, because Pip feels guilty throughout the novel. But then we realised that was too big for twenty minutes.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: So we decided on social class and ambition. They're connected, because Pip wants to become a gentleman, and that's what drives most of the plot.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: A wise decision. Those two themes together give you a clear argument. Guilt would have been a mistake in so short a time.

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: I also considered crime, because of Magwitch. But I think that belongs to a different essay.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Quite right. Have you read any critical writing on the novel, or only the text itself?

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: Two articles. One argues that Pip is a snob, and the other says he's simply a young man who is easily influenced by those around him. I find the second one more convincing.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: I'm not so sure. I think he has a choice, and he makes bad choices. But I'd rather present both views and let the audience decide.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: That's the right approach, as long as you say which one you favour at the end. A presentation without a position is rather dull. Also, give the full details of each article on a final slide. Now, let's talk about the characters. How will you use them?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Pip, obviously, is the centre. His ambition makes him leave his family and become, in a way, ashamed of them.

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: And Miss Havisham shows how the past can control a person. She stops all the clocks on the day she was left at the altar, and she never moves on.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: I'd also like to discuss Magwitch. He seems frightening at the beginning, but later we learn that he has been secretly paying for Pip's education. His generosity is hidden, and Pip finds it humiliating.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: That's a strong analysis. I'd say Magwitch is the most interesting of the three, and don't be afraid to spend more time on him. So, what about your slides?

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: We've prepared twelve. I tried to put quotations on most of them.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Hmm. That may be too many. Twelve slides is fine for twenty minutes, but you have a lot of words on each. When people read the screen they stop listening to you. Cut the text by half, and use quotations only when you really need them.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: I had thought the text was too small, too, but Zainab says it's all right on the projector. She also wants to include a picture of the author, which I think is a waste of space.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: I'd agree. A picture adds little. Keep the space for ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: It's not the size so much as the amount. Another thing is the colour. The dark red background is hard to read. Choose something lighter.

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: I'll change that tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: And finally, practise out loud. Time yourselves. Most students go over time, and then the end of the talk is rushed. The conclusion is what the audience remembers.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: We're going to rehearse on Thursday, in the seminar room.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Good idea. Also, think about who will speak when. Don't just alternate every slide. Divide it by sections, so each of you owns a part.

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: I'll do the introduction and the part on class, and Tom will take ambition and the conclusion.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: That works for me.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: One more practical point. Will you take questions during the talk or after it?

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: After, I think. If people interrupt in the middle, we'll lose time.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: But a few questions in the middle could help us check that people are following. Maybe we could stop once, halfway.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: I like that. Plan one pause, after the section on class. It also gives you a breath. And what is your final sentence?

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: We haven't decided.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: I'd like to finish with a quotation from the last chapter.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Good, but choose a short one, something the audience can remember.

transcript.speaker: Dr Brennan
transcript.text: Excellent. I'm looking forward to it. Don't forget, the presentation is on the twelfth, at two o'clock, and I'll be sitting at the back. Good luck.

transcript.speaker: Zainab
transcript.text: Thank you, Dr Brennan.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Thanks. See you on the twelfth.

sections.title: The geology of the Giant's Causeway
sections.context: You will hear a geology lecturer talking about a famous rock formation on the coast of Northern Ireland.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture I want to take you to the north coast of Northern Ireland, to a place that looks as though it was built by giants: the Giant's Causeway. It's one of the most visited natural sites in the British Isles, and it's also a wonderful example of how geology and legend can explain the same landscape in two very different ways. I'll start with the science.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The story begins about 60 million years ago, at a time when this part of the world was very different. The Atlantic Ocean was just beginning to open, as the continents of Europe and North America slowly moved apart. As they did so, the Earth's crust was stretched and cracked, and molten rock from deep underground forced its way to the surface. For several million years there were huge volcanic eruptions across the area that is now Antrim.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The rock that flowed out was a kind of lava called basalt. Basalt is dark, very fluid, and it runs a long way before it stops. It poured out in sheets, filling valleys and covering the older rocks. Over time, layer upon layer built up, and today those layers form high plateaus along the coast.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now to the columns. The Causeway is made of about 40,000 of them, packed tightly together like the cells of a honeycomb. Most of the columns have six sides, though some have four, five, seven or even eight. The tallest are about 12 metres high, and the rock is so regular that visitors often find it hard to believe nature made it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: How did that happen? When the thick lava flow began to cool, it also began to shrink. Think of what happens when you leave a bowl of wet clay in the sun. It dries, and as it dries it contracts. If it can't shrink evenly, it cracks. The same process occurred in the lava. As it cooled from the top and the bottom, it contracted, and cracks formed in the shape of hexagons. Then the cracks slowly grew downward through the rock, forming the columns.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That analogy with drying mud is not simply a nice comparison. Scientists have actually done experiments with wet starch, and they produce miniature columns that look remarkably like the real thing. In both cases, the cracks tend to meet at angles of about one hundred and twenty degrees, which is exactly what you find at the Causeway.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So much for the science. What about the legend? According to the old story, the Irish giant Finn McCool built the causeway as a path across the sea to Scotland, because he wanted to fight a rival giant who lived there. When Finn reached the other side, he found that the Scottish giant was much bigger than he was. Finn ran home, and his wife disguised him as a baby. When the Scottish giant saw how large the baby was, he thought the father must be enormous, and he fled, tearing up the causeway behind him. The story is told a little differently in different villages, and in some versions it is Finn's rival who builds the bridge.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Of course, it's a legend, but there is a surprising link with real geology. Across the sea in Scotland, on the small island of Staffa, you can find exactly the same kind of columns, from the very same lava flow. Fingal's Cave, on Staffa, is a sea cave lined with basalt columns. So the story of a bridge between the two countries isn't completely wild. The two places were once part of the same landscape.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let me turn to protection. The Causeway was named a World Heritage Site in 1986. Recognition like that brings visitors, and today about 1 million people come every year. That creates problems of its own. The columns can be damaged by walking, and rare plants grow in the cracks. The managers have built paths, and visitors are asked to keep to them, but pressure remains.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The site is managed by a charity, which depends on money from its visitor centre. The centre has exhibitions that explain the geology, a café and a shop. Many visitors buy a ticket for the centre and never realise that the path along the shore is open to everyone.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's another threat which can't be controlled by paths, and that is the sea. Waves have been eroding the coast for thousands of years, and storms are growing stronger. A number of columns have already fallen. Monitoring teams use laser scanners every year to measure how fast the cliffs retreat.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: I'd like to leave you with a question. Why do you think so many cultures produce legends about places like this? My own view is that when the shapes of nature seem too perfect, people look for a human explanation. We'll talk about this further in the seminar, and I'd like you to read the article on the reading list before then.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next week, we'll move on from Ireland to Iceland, where the same process of crust-stretching can still be seen. Please come to the lecture with the notes from today, because we'll compare the two places in detail.
